opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was around 2019 and 2020, when I was just starting my PhD at Princeton. Text-based games like Zork had been around for decades, and people had been building reinforcement learning agents for them for a few years. But I always felt something was off about how those agents worked.

These games are basically pure language. You read a description, "you're in a dark room, there's a lamp on the table," and you type something like "take lamp" or "go north." The action space is open-ended language. But most RL approaches at the time either relied on a handcrafted list of valid actions, or tried to learn language from scratch through the game's reward signal. That's incredibly inefficient. Imagine learning English just by playing Zork and getting points occasionally. It's almost impossible.

Then GPT-2 came out, and it was the first time you had a model that seemed to carry real priors about language and about the world. If you're in a room with a lamp, it has some sense that "take lamp" or "turn on lamp" is reasonable and "eat lamp" probably isn't. So the natural idea was: what if the language model proposes plausible actions, and the RL agent learns which ones are actually good in this particular game? That became our paper, CALM. The language model handles the common sense, and RL handles the game-specific decisions.

Looking back, I think the deeper motivation was that I believed these games are a microcosm of something bigger. Language isn't just for describing things. It's a way to act in the world. If you want agents that can do general things, they need to reason and act through language. Text games were the cleanest testbed for that, and GPT-2 was the first sign that language models might give agents the prior knowledge they'd always been missing.

Of course, GPT-2 was still pretty weak, and we also found that the agents weren't really "understanding" the text in the way you'd hope. In a follow-up we showed you could scramble the semantics and some agents did about as well, which was humbling. But that was part of what made it interesting. It made me think the bottleneck was really about reasoning, and that line of thinking eventually led to work like ReAct.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using GPT-2’s language knowledge to suggest plausible actions in text-based games, with reinforcement learning learning which actions work well in the game.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it started from a kind of dissatisfaction rather than a grand plan. When I was at Princeton around 2019 and 2020, the dominant paradigm for sequential decision-making was still reinforcement learning on games, Atari, MuJoCo, that sort of thing. Those environments are beautiful for studying control, but the observation and action spaces are low-level pixels or joint torques. There's very little of what makes human decision-making interesting, which is that we reason over abstract concepts and communicate in language.

Text games like Zork had been around forever, and people in NLP had already tried training RL agents on them, but the results were honestly a bit sad. The agents were basically learning to memorize trajectories. You'd put them in a new game and they'd fall apart, because they had no prior about what a "kitchen" or a "key" even is. Every word was just a token to be ground out through millions of trial-and-error steps.

So when GPT-2 came out, what struck me wasn't the generation quality per se. It was that for the first time there was a model that already carried a huge amount of commonsense about how the world works, encoded in language. If you're in a text game and you see "there is a locked chest here," a language model already knows that chests open with keys and that you might want to look for one. An RL agent from scratch has to discover that from reward signal, which is incredibly sample-inefficient.

The bet was pretty simple: what if the hard part of these games, generating sensible candidate actions, could be offloaded to a language model, and the RL part only had to learn which of a few plausible actions to pick? That became the CALM paper, where we fine-tuned GPT-2 on human gameplay transcripts and used it as an action generator. And it worked surprisingly well, it generalized to unseen games in a way earlier methods didn't.

But the deeper reason I thought it was worth revisiting is that I saw text games as a testbed for something bigger. I didn't really care about Zork. I cared about the question: can language models be agents? Can they take actions in an environment, observe consequences, and adapt? Text games were just the simplest, cheapest sandbox to ask that question. And in hindsight, that line of thinking led pretty directly to WebShop, to ReAct, to everything after. The models got stronger, the environments got more realistic, but the core question stayed the same.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using GPT-2’s commonsense to generate sensible actions in text games, with reinforcement learning choosing among them, and says this approach worked well.

astra-6.text:
The motivation was that language games combine two things: understanding language and acting in an environment. You don’t just read a description and answer a question—you choose an action, observe what happens, and use that feedback to make progress.

With a model like GPT-2, we could revisit how much prior language knowledge helps with that process. For example, the model might already have some intuition that a key can unlock a door, instead of having to learn every relationship through trial and error. But knowing what an action means is different from knowing whether it’s useful in the current situation.

So the interesting question was how to connect that language knowledge with learning from interaction. Could a language model suggest plausible actions, while an agent learns which ones actually lead to progress? Language games offered a relatively simple setting to study that connection.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-2’s prior language knowledge might help an agent learn from interaction, but it does not clearly raise the comparative hypothesis that stronger language models might be better at playing text-based games.

sol-6.1.text:
What interested me was that language games give us a way to study language as part of acting. The agent has to read a description, infer what situation it’s in, and choose an action that changes that situation. So understanding the words is only part of the problem—you also need memory, exploration, and planning.

With models like GPT-2, it seemed worth asking whether pretrained language knowledge could help with that. For example, if you see a locked door and you have a key, you already have some intuition about what to try. An agent learning from scratch might need many interactions to discover that. The question was whether we could use those language priors to make learning more efficient, while still letting interaction with the game determine which actions actually work.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether pretrained language knowledge from models like GPT-2 could help agents learn to act in language games more efficiently, conveying the hypothesis that stronger language models may improve text-game play.
